analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal nursing home inspections by requiring tougher inspector testing, adequate inspection staffing, whistleblower protections, and penalties for pressuring inspectors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have tightened federal oversight of nursing home inspections, never received a committee vote or House vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing home inspectors — called surveyors — are the officials who check facilities for problems that could harm residents. This bill would have required tougher testing and continuing education for those inspectors, required states to employ enough qualified inspectors to do the job, made it illegal for anyone, including nursing home operators or elected officials, to pressure an inspector to change findings (with penalties up to $10,000), and protected inspectors from retaliation if they reported problems. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, who rely on federal and state inspections to catch unsafe or poor-quality care. Roughly 1.4 million people live in nursing homes, nearly all paid for through Medicare or Medicaid. The bill would also protect the inspectors themselves through whistleblower protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires that the tests nursing home inspectors must pass be rigorous enough to ensure facilities are surveyed consistently and accurately.

Directs HHS to set qualification and pay standards for survey teams and to require states to employ enough inspectors to actually oversee the facilities in their state, plus regular continuing education for inspectors.
Requires inspectors to report any survey that underreports problems affecting resident safety, and protects them from being fired, demoted, or harassed for reporting.

Creates civil money penalties up to $10,000 for anyone — including nursing home employees, industry representatives, or elected officials — who tries to improperly influence an inspection, and up to $50,000 for state officials who retaliate against inspectors.

Establishes an advisory committee including resident advocates, surveyors, and nursing home administrators to recommend standards on staffing, training, and limiting contact between inspectors and facility interests, and requires supervisory review of each survey.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators would face a greater risk of accurate, unfavorable inspection findings and associated penalties; state governments would bear the cost of hiring and training enough qualified inspectors; facility staff and officials who try to sway inspectors would face fines up to $10,000.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and state agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves nearly every standard — how rigorous testing must be, what 'adequate' staffing means, what counts as 'inappropriate influence' — to be defined later by the HHS Secretary, so its real-world strength would depend entirely on future regulation.

It imposes new training, staffing, and reporting obligations on state survey agencies, which states would have to fund, and imposes penalty exposure on facility staff, industry representatives, and even elected officials who try to sway survey results.

Critics of stricter survey enforcement generally argue it adds compliance and litigation costs for nursing homes, costs that largely fall on an industry already operating on thin Medicaid margins — though the bill does not directly change facility reimbursement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real: independent, well-staffed inspectors are the main safeguard between residents and substandard care, and requiring states to employ enough qualified surveyors addresses a chronic understaffing problem. The costs are modest and fall on nursing home operators and state agencies rather than taxpayers in any large way. The bill is light on specifics — it delegates most standards to the HHS Secretary — and some might argue existing survey rules already cover training, making parts duplicative. On balance a low-cost bill aimed at a genuine safety gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, and it never got a markup or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard introduced the bill on July 30, 2013; it was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees.
On August 2, 2013 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action followed.
The bill attracted no cosponsors, and it died at the end of the 113th Congress without a committee vote or a House floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators are better off, since inspections that determine penalties and Medicare/Medicaid compliance remain as vulnerable to understaffing and pressure as before; the bill would also have imposed new duties on state agencies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators facing weaker inspections

for.name: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it received no cosponsors and no committee action beyond referral.

for.name: House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or advanced it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Democrat, supported the bill and no one opposed it on the record; the bill died quietly in committee without any recorded votes, so no partisan split was ever visible.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and their corporate operators
industries.note: The bill makes it harder to soften or underreport the results of the inspections that determine nursing homes' Medicare and Medicaid participation and penalties, raising the risk of enforcement for substandard facilities. Residents and their families gain the corresponding protection.

industries.industry: State survey agencies and their employees
industries.note: State inspection staff gain whistleblower protections, required compensation standards, and continuing education, but also take on mandatory reporting duties and new federal staffing requirements that states must resource.
